(CNN) -- Nicaragua President Daniel Ortega said Thursday that the nation is breaking relations with Colombia "in solidarity with the Ecuadoran people." The move comes after the Organization of American States passed a resolution Wednesday in hopes of easing tensions stemming from an attack by Colombian military on a rebel camp in neighboring Ecuador on Saturday. Since that attack, Ecuador has broken off relations with Colombia, and Venezuela says it has moved troops to its border with Colombia. Ortega made his televised remarks in Managua, where he was flanked by Ecuadoran President Rafael Correa. Colombian forces killed at least 17 members of the leftist group Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia on Saturday. FARC is estimated to be holding at least 700 hostages in the jungles of Colombia and has been accused by the United States of being a terrorist organization. "This rupture of relations isn't with the people of Colombia," Ortega said. "We are breaking with the terrorist policies that the government of [Colombian President] Alvaro Uribe is practicing." In its resolution, the OAS called the attack "a violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ecuador and of principles of international law." It ordered a commission, headed by OAS Secretary-General Jose Miguel Insulza and composed of four ambassadors designated by him, to visit both countries to investigate the matter, "and to propose formulas for bringing the two nations closer together." Colombian officials have apologized for taking their attack against the leftist Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia into Ecuador but said it was necessary to counter a threat to their national security. Colombian officials also said they discovered evidence after the attack that Ecuadoran and Venezuelan government officials were collaborating with the group -- namely that Chavez allegedly gave $300 million to the rebels and that a senior Ecuadoran official met with them. "[They] are making things up and there's no limit to what they'll make up," Chavez said at a news conference on Wednesday. Correa has said his country would only be satisfied when the OAS issues a "clear condemnation" against Colombia for the raid. OAS foreign ministers are to meet March 17 in Washington "to examine the facts and make the pertinent recommendations," the resolution concluded. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said Wednesday that he saw little chance of war erupting between Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela.  Learn more about the countries » . Gates added that the United States would not need to assist its Colombian allies should armed conflict break out. "My personal view is that there is relatively little likelihood of a military conflict between them, and my further impression is that the Colombians can take care of themselves," he said at the Pentagon. (CNN) — Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega said Thursday that his nation is severing diplomatic relations with Colombia “in solidarity with the Ecuadoran people.”

Ortega’s announcement came after the Organization of American States passed a resolution Wednesday aimed at easing tensions following a Colombian military attack on a rebel camp in neighboring Ecuador on Saturday. Since the attack, Ecuador has broken off relations with Colombia, and Venezuela says it has moved troops to its border with Colombia.

Ortega made the televised remarks in Managua, where he was joined by Ecuadoran President Rafael Correa.

Colombian forces killed at least 17 members of the leftist Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, on Saturday. The group is estimated to be holding at least 700 hostages in Colombia’s jungles and has been designated by the United States as a terrorist organization.

“This rupture of relations isn’t with the people of Colombia,” Ortega said. “We are breaking with the terrorist policies that the government of [Colombian President] Alvaro Uribe is practicing.”

In its resolution, the OAS called the attack “a violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ecuador and of principles of international law.” It ordered a commission, led by OAS Secretary-General Jose Miguel Insulza and composed of four ambassadors designated by him, to visit both countries to investigate the matter “and to propose formulas for bringing the two nations closer together.”

Colombian officials have apologized for extending their operation against FARC into Ecuador but said the action was necessary to counter a threat to their national security. They also said they discovered evidence after the attack that Ecuadoran and Venezuelan government officials were collaborating with the group — specifically, that Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez allegedly gave $300 million to the rebels and that a senior Ecuadoran official met with them.

“[They] are making things up, and there’s no limit to what they’ll make up,” Chavez said at a news conference Wednesday.

Correa has said his country would be satisfied only when the OAS issues a “clear condemnation” of Colombia for the raid.

OAS foreign ministers are scheduled to meet March 17 in Washington “to examine the facts and make the pertinent recommendations,” the resolution concluded.

U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said Wednesday that he saw little chance of war erupting among Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela. Gates added that the United States would not need to assist its Colombian allies should armed conflict break out.

“My personal view is that there is relatively little likelihood of a military conflict between them, and my further impression is that the Colombians can take care of themselves,” he said at the Pentagon.

**MANAGUA, Nicaragua** — Nicaragua has severed diplomatic relations with Colombia in a show of solidarity with Ecuador, escalating a regional crisis sparked by a Colombian military raid on a FARC rebel camp inside Ecuadorian territory.

Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega announced the decision Thursday, condemning the cross-border operation as a violation of Ecuador’s sovereignty. The raid, carried out by Colombian forces, killed senior FARC commander Raúl Reyes and several others.

“We are breaking relations with the terrorist government of Álvaro Uribe,” Ortega said, referring to Colombia’s president. He said Nicaragua was acting in support of Ecuador, which has already cut diplomatic ties with Bogotá.

Colombia has defended the raid, saying it targeted members of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, a guerrilla group that has fought the Colombian government for decades and is designated a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union.

But Ecuador called the operation an unacceptable incursion onto its soil. President Rafael Correa ordered Colombian diplomats expelled and deployed troops to the border, demanding an apology from Bogotá.

The dispute has drawn in other regional governments. Venezuela also condemned Colombia’s actions and moved troops toward its border with Colombia, raising concerns about a broader diplomatic and military standoff in South America.

Colombian officials have said documents recovered from the FARC camp indicate links between the rebel group and some neighboring governments — allegations Ecuador and Venezuela have denied.

The Organization of American States has called for restraint and urged the countries involved to seek a diplomatic resolution.

Nicaragua’s move adds another layer to the crisis, though the country does not share a land border with Colombia. Relations between Managua and Bogotá have long been strained by a maritime territorial dispute in the Caribbean.

The Colombian raid has become one of the most serious diplomatic confrontations in Latin America in years, testing regional alliances and raising questions about how far governments can go in pursuing armed groups across international borders.

**WASHINGTON/BOGOTA, March 2008 (Wire report)** — A Colombian military strike on a guerrilla camp inside Ecuador triggered one of Latin America’s sharpest diplomatic crises in years, drawing Ecuador, Venezuela and Nicaragua into a confrontation with Bogotá and prompting an emergency response from the Organization of American States.

The crisis began March 1, 2008, when Colombian forces crossed into Ecuadorian territory and attacked a jungle encampment used by the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC. The raid killed senior FARC commander Raúl Reyes and more than 20 others. Colombia said the operation was a legitimate act of self-defense against a guerrilla group responsible for kidnappings, bombings and attacks inside Colombia.

Ecuador denounced the raid as a violation of its sovereignty and broke diplomatic relations with Colombia. President Rafael Correa accused Bogotá of deliberately attacking Ecuadorian territory and said Colombia had misled Quito about the nature of the operation.

Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez responded by ordering troops toward the Colombian border and expelling Colombian diplomats, warning Bogotá against any similar action on Venezuelan soil. Colombia in turn accused Chávez and Ecuadorian officials of maintaining improper contacts with the FARC, citing material it said was recovered from computers seized in the raid.

Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega joined the diplomatic offensive against Colombia, announcing that Nicaragua was breaking relations with Bogotá in solidarity with Ecuador. Ortega sharply criticized Colombian President Álvaro Uribe and portrayed the cross-border strike as an act of aggression against a sovereign state. His move also came amid longstanding Nicaraguan-Colombian tensions over maritime claims in the Caribbean.

The Organization of American States convened an emergency meeting in Washington. In a resolution approved by member states, the OAS said Colombia’s incursion violated Ecuador’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and reaffirmed the principle that no state may violate another’s territory. The body stopped short of imposing sanctions, instead calling for dialogue and sending a fact-finding mission. The OAS also convened a meeting of foreign ministers to address the dispute.

The United States, Colombia’s closest ally in the region, expressed support for Uribe’s government while urging a diplomatic solution. U.S. officials said Colombia had the right to defend itself against the FARC, which Washington designates as a terrorist organization, but also called for respect for regional stability and a peaceful resolution through the OAS. Washington criticized Venezuela’s troop movements and warned against escalation.

Tensions eased days later at a Rio Group summit in Santo Domingo, where Uribe, Correa and Chávez publicly exchanged words but ultimately agreed to lower the temperature. Uribe apologized for the violation of Ecuadorian territory, while defending the raid as necessary against the FARC. The leaders shook hands, and Venezuela and Ecuador later pulled back from the brink of military confrontation, though diplomatic distrust lingered.

The raid, carried out by Colombian forces inside Ecuadorian territory, killed senior FARC commander Raúl Reyes and other guerrillas. Colombia defended the operation as a necessary action against a dangerous insurgent group that it said used remote border areas as safe havens. But Ecuador denounced the attack as a violation of its sovereignty, saying Colombian troops had entered its territory without permission.

Ecuador’s president, Rafael Correa, reacted angrily, breaking diplomatic ties with Colombia and ordering troops toward the border. He accused Bogotá of deliberately violating international law and demanded regional condemnation. Correa also rejected Colombian claims that his government had any improper relationship with the FARC.

Venezuela’s president, Hugo Chávez, quickly sided with Ecuador. He condemned Colombia’s action, expelled Colombian diplomats, and ordered Venezuelan forces to the Colombian border. Chávez warned that a similar Colombian operation on Venezuelan soil could lead to war, sharply escalating tensions in the Andean region.

Colombia, led at the time by President Álvaro Uribe, countered by saying evidence recovered from computers found at the FARC camp suggested contacts between the rebels and officials in Ecuador and Venezuela. Those allegations further inflamed the dispute, though Ecuador and Venezuela denied supporting the guerrillas.

The crisis moved to the Organization of American States, where member states debated how to respond. The OAS approved a resolution recognizing that Colombia had violated Ecuador’s sovereignty and reaffirming the principle that no state should conduct military operations inside another country without consent. The resolution stopped short of imposing harsh sanctions on Colombia, reflecting a compromise aimed at easing tensions while acknowledging Ecuador’s complaint.

U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates, visiting the region soon afterward, expressed support for Colombia’s fight against the FARC and emphasized that the guerrilla group remained a serious security threat. At the same time, the United States backed diplomatic efforts to calm the standoff and avoid a broader confrontation among Colombia, Ecuador, and Venezuela.

The immediate aftermath was marked by troop movements, diplomatic expulsions, emergency regional meetings, and accusations on all sides. However, despite the fierce rhetoric from Hugo Chávez and Rafael Correa and the seriousness of the OAS resolution, the crisis did not develop into open conflict. ## Nicaragua severs diplomatic relations with Colombia after cross-border raid in Ecuador

**MANAGUA, Nicaragua —** Nicaragua has severed diplomatic relations with Colombia in protest over a Colombian military raid on a rebel camp inside Ecuador, escalating a regional crisis that has drawn sharp reactions across Latin America.

Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega announced the move Thursday, saying his government was breaking ties “in solidarity with the people and government of Ecuador” after Colombian forces crossed into Ecuadorian territory to attack a camp used by the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, known as the FARC.

“We are breaking diplomatic relations with the terrorist government of Álvaro Uribe,” Ortega said, referring to Colombia’s president. He accused Colombia of violating Ecuador’s sovereignty and warned that the raid set a dangerous precedent for the region.

Colombia has defended the operation, saying its forces targeted a senior FARC commander who had used the camp as a base for planning attacks and hostage operations. Colombian officials said the raid killed Raúl Reyes, one of the guerrilla group’s top leaders, along with more than a dozen others.

“This was an action in legitimate defense against a terrorist organization,” Colombian officials said after the operation, arguing that the FARC had long used remote border areas to evade Colombian security forces.

Ecuador’s government denounced the raid as an incursion onto its territory and cut diplomatic relations with Colombia earlier this week. President Rafael Correa said the attack was carried out without Ecuador’s permission and accused Bogotá of misleading his government.

“This was not a pursuit. It was a massacre,” Correa said, insisting that the rebels were bombed while they slept and that Colombian troops later entered Ecuadorian territory to remove Reyes’ body.

The Colombian strike has triggered one of the most serious diplomatic disputes in South America in years. Venezuela’s President Hugo Chávez, a close ally of both Ortega and Correa, also condemned the raid and ordered troops toward Colombia’s border, warning that a similar attack on Venezuelan soil would be considered an act of war.

Colombia, meanwhile, has said documents recovered from computers at the FARC camp suggest links between the rebel group and officials in neighboring countries, allegations Ecuador and Venezuela have rejected as politically motivated.

The FARC, Latin America’s oldest guerrilla insurgency, has fought the Colombian government for decades. The group, founded in the 1960s as a Marxist peasant movement, has been widely accused of kidnappings, bombings, drug trafficking and attacks on civilians. Colombia, the United States and the European Union have designated the FARC as a terrorist organization.

The raid that killed Reyes was a major victory for Uribe’s U.S.-backed security strategy, which has focused on weakening the FARC militarily and recovering state control over areas once dominated by rebels. But the decision to strike across an international border has prompted accusations that Colombia violated international law.

Regional governments have called for restraint and dialogue. The Organization of American States has taken up the dispute, with several members urging a diplomatic solution to prevent the crisis from widening.

Nicaragua’s decision adds another layer to the standoff, though its practical effect may be limited compared with Ecuador’s rupture in relations with Colombia. Still, Ortega’s announcement signals a broader political alignment in the region, with leftist governments rallying behind Ecuador and criticizing Colombia’s close security ties with Washington.

Colombia has said it does not seek conflict with its neighbors and remains focused on combating the FARC.

“We have not violated sovereignty out of ambition or hostility,” Colombian officials said. “Our goal is to protect Colombians from terrorism.”

But Ecuador, Nicaragua and Venezuela say the issue is not Colombia’s fight against rebels, but whether one country can launch military operations inside another without consent.

“The sovereignty of a nation must be respected,” Ortega said. “If this is allowed, no country in Latin America is safe.”
